Atypical low back pain: stiff-person syndrome
Philippe Gallien1*, Aurélie Durufle, Sabine Petrilli1, Marc Verin2, Régine Brissot1,
Sandrine Robineau1
1
Service de rééducation fonctionnelle CHU Pontchaillou, rue Henri Le Guillou 35 033 Rennes Cedex, France; 2service
de Neurologie CHU Pontchaillou, rue Henri Le Guillou 35 033 Rennes Cedex, France
(Submitted for publication August 17, 2000; accepted in revised form April 4, 2001)

Summary – Stiff-person syndrome was diagnosed in a patient with chronic low back pain. The diagnosis
of this rare neurological condition rests mainly on the clinical findings of axial and proximal limb rigidity,
increased lumbar lordosis often accompanied with pain, and normal neurological findings apart from brisk
deep tendon reflexes. Electromyography of the lumbar paraspinal muscles shows motor unit firing at rest
with normal appearance of the motor unit potentials. Titers of antibody to glutamic acid decarboxylase are
elevated. Diazepam is the treatment of reference. Physical therapy can substantially improve quality of life.

back pain / physical therapy / stiff-person syndrome

Stiff-person syndrome is a rare neurological condition
first described in 1956 by Moersch and Woltman under
the name “stiff man syndrome” [1, 2]. Rigidity and
episodic spasms predominating at the trunk and girdles
are the characteristic symptoms. Rigidity of the lumbar
paraspinal muscles causes an increase in lumbar lordosis
with low back pain, which is among the most common
presenting symptoms. We report a case in a 35-year-old
woman and present a literature review on the diagnosis
and management of stiff-person syndrome.
CASE-REPORT
A 35-year-old woman was referred to our outpatient
clinic for a two-year history of low back pain that
started insidiously, initially with a mechanical time
pattern. The pain worsened gradually until it became
continuous, with no exacerbation during coughing.

She also reported a gradual deepening of her lumbar
spine curvature that tilted her sacrum to an increasingly
horizontal position. Her family confirmed this change.
Her medical history was unremarkable. During the two
years since the onset of her pain, she had blood tests,
which disclosed no evidence of inflammation or metabolic disease. Plain radiographs and a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the lumbar spine showed
increased lordosis with facet joint impingement. Analgesics, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents, physical
therapy, and immobilization in a plaster cast had failed
to relieve the pain.
Lumbar hyperlordosis was the most striking physical
finding at presentation to our clinic. The L3-wall distance was 12 cm and the T6-wall distance 6 cm, indicating that the thoracic spine was stooped forward.
Passive hyperextension of the lumbar spine replicated
the severe pain described by the patient, whereas
decreasing the lumbar curvature alleviated the pain.
The only abnormal neurological findings were rigidity
of the paraspinal, abdominal, and proximal right lower

limb muscles. All the deep tendon reflexes at all four
limbs were brisk, although there was no diffusion.
Other physical findings were normal. An electrophysiological study showed normal conduction velocities in
the common peroneal nerve (51. 7 m/s), median nerve
(70 m/s), sural nerve (49. 6 m/s), and radial nerve
(60. 7 m/s). Needle detection in the paraspinal muscles
at T2/T4, T8/T9, L2/L3, and L4/L5 showed nearly
continuous motor unit firing; the motor unit potentials
were small, and few were polyphasic (figure 1). Potentials related to volitional contraction were superimposed on this background. Needle detection at the
deltoid and tibialis anterior muscle was normal.
Findings were normal from standard laboratory tests
including serum electrolytes, muscle enzymes, liver
function tests, thyroid hormones, acute-phase reactants, and glucose. Examination of the cerebrospinal
fluid was normal. The titer of antibody to glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD) determined by radioimmunoassay was elevated to 1. 35 (normal, < 0. 11). Tests were
negative for anti-tissue antibodies (smooth muscle,
mitochondria, LKM1, cytosol, and parietal cells). Also
negative were tests for anti-thyroid, anti-DNA, and
anti-ENA antibodies. A second MRI scan was normal.
Stiff-person syndrome was diagnosed based on the
following arguments: axial rigidity, increased lumbar
lordosis, normal motor and sensory function, normal
cognitive function, continuous paraspinal muscle activity at rest, and a positive titer of anti-GAD antibodies.
Oral diazepam was started but induced vertigo and
drowsiness that were unacceptable to the patient. A
day-hospital program of physical therapy was undertaken; it involved stretching of all posterior muscle

planes, postural awareness exercises to decrease the
lumbar lordosis, and analgesic pool therapy with water
jets to induce muscle relaxation. After one month, the
patient was pain-free and the lumbar curvature was
substantially decreased, with an L3-wall distance of
8 cm and a T6-wall distance of 4 cm. A home exercise
program conducted under the supervision of a physical
therapist was started. Findings one year later showed
that the therapeutic benefits were sustained, with good
control of the pain, an L3-wall distance of 9 cm and a
T6-wall distance of 2 cm.
DISCUSSION
Stiff-person syndrome is a rare cause of low back pain
that physicians should bear in mind [2-5]. The onset is
insidious and the symptoms worsen slowly. The first
complaint is usually mechanical pain located low in the
lumbar spine and related to the increased lumbar lordosis induced by the paraspinal muscle rigidity. Superimposed episodic spasms triggered by noise, emotions,
and passive movement occur in some patients. This was
the only classic symptom lacking in our patient. Spasms
were also absent in one of the patients described by
Barker [3]. One possibility is that our patient was seen
before the occurrence of spasms, which may appear late
in the course of this very slowly progressive disease.
Motor and sensory function is normal, although briskness of the deep tendon reflexes is common. Cognitive
function and sphincter function were normal in all the
cases reported to date; presence of these symptoms
should suggest stiff-limb syndrome or progressive
encephalomyelitis, which are related conditions but

have a far worse prognosis [3-6]. In stiff-limb syndrome, the rigidity predominates in the lower limbs,
and the presenting symptom is often rigidity of the
ankle or foot, whereas axial rigidity and increased lumbar lordosis are uncommon. Urinary symptoms often
develop during the course of the disease. Antibodies to
GAD are usually negative. Electrophysiological studies
show continuous firing at rest in the affected muscles,
but the motor unit potentials have an abnormal,
polyphasic appearance. Progressive encephalomyelitis
manifests as rigidity of the trunk and limbs with rapid
involvement of the cortex and medulla oblongata.
Death usually occurs within two to three years.
Black [7] reported that many patients with stiffperson syndrome had psychiatric conditions, particularly depression. Physicians who monitor these patients
should be alert to the possibility of psychiatric decompensation. The diagnosis is suspected based on the
clinical findings and is confirmed by the continuous
motor unit firing with normal-appearing motor unit
potentials from the paraspinal muscles [2, 3]. Elevated
titers of antibodies to GAD are present in 60% of
patients, suggesting that autoimmunity is involved [3,
5, 8, 9, 10]. One hypothesis is that an abnormality in
the metabolism of gamma aminobutyric acid may
impair inhibitory inputs to motor neurons [4]. Patients
should be tested routinely for insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, which is present in one-third of cases.
Stiff-person syndrome has also been reported in patients
with lung or colon cancer or with Hodgkin disease [2,
3, 4, 5, 11, 12], many of whom had positive tests for
anti-amphiphysin antibodies [11, 13]. However, paraneoplastic forms are more common among patients
with stiff-limb syndrome [3, 11, 13], which manifests
as painful rigidity of the trunk and distal limb muscles,
particularly at the lower limbs, with muscle spasm. Half
the patients have cognitive disorders and sphincter
dysfunction. Elevation of anti-GAD titers is far less
common than in stiff-person syndrome. Treatment of
the malignancy can improve the neurological manifestations.
The prognosis is better in stiff-person syndrome than
in stiff-limb syndrome. In the study by Barker et al. [3],
all the patients with pure axial involvement remained
able to walk, whereas six of the 13 patients with stifflimb syndrome were wheelchair bound 31⁄2 years after
symptom onset. Of the 13 patients studied by Lorish et
al. [2], 11 were still self-sufficient after one to 28 years
and the other two had died, one of septicemia with
renal failure and the other suddenly during a muscle

spasm. Various treatments have been suggested.
Although diazepam is currently the treatment of reference, the high dosages required to achieve a therapeutic
effect (20 to 300 mg) can induce drowsiness [2, 3]. Oral
baclofen has been advocated, and intrathecal injections
of baclofen have been used with variable results [14].
Because the pathophysiology of the disease seems to
involve autoimmunity, immunosuppressive and immunomodulating agents have been tried, including glucocorticoids and intravenous immunoglobulins, again
with variable results [2, 3, 15]. Levodopa worsens the
symptoms [2]. Our case shows that rehabilitation
therapy is valuable. Stretching, lordosis reduction, and
physiotherapy induced substantial improvements. Lorish et al. [2] are the only other authors who have
underlined the usefulness of rehabilitation therapy in
stiff-person syndrome. Rehabilitation therapy should
be started early to reduce the need for medications,
since these can induce severe drowsiness.
